title: EU: Countries Plan Rwanda Deportation Centers
content:
(Brussels) – Negotiations to set up an offshore deportation center in Rwanda, which has a shocking human rights record, are a particularly cruel departure from the founding values of the European Union, Human Rights Watch said today.

After months of speculation, Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece, and the Netherlands, alongside Rwanda’s interior minister, confirmed the negotiations on November 16, 2026, on the sidelines of the Vienna Migration Conference organized by the International Centre for Migration Policy Development. The five EU countries confirmed their plan to send people whose asylum claims have been rejected in the EU to Rwanda starting in 2027.

“History has shown that third country transfers violate rights and cause suffering,” said Judith Sunderland, senior associate refugee and migrant rights director at Human Rights Watch. “The choice of a country that has an abysmal human rights record and resists international scrutiny tracks with that history and evokes deep skepticism that any nominal rights safeguards will be respected.”

title: The Students Beat the Strongman. Now What? Five Questions on What Comes Next For Serbia
content:
A new political party organized by student protesters made history last month when it ousted Serbia’s longtime leader Aleksandar Vučić at the polls, ending his party’s 14-year stranglehold on power. 

Long seen as immovable, Vučić was defeated by students who managed to rally support from across the country around a central, unifying goal: freeing Serbia’s institutions and economy from the corruption that flourished under the rule of his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS). 

Their electoral victory was decisive and undeniable. But dismantling the former regime’s networks of influence will not be easy. Serbia’s democratic credentials deteriorated under Vučić, with the leader and his party accused of cultivating extensive patronage networks inside the country’s judiciary, security forces, media, and private sector. 

The students, whose leaderless protest movement selected a range of political novices to represent them in parliament under the banner of the “Student List,” have vowed to restore independence to state bodies and end impunity for the corrupt.

title: Behold the Gloriously Cheap 1970s Italian Knockoffs Inspired by Star Wars
content:
When the first Star Wars movie came out, in 1977, cinema was the better part of a century old, yet it had never produced a popular-culture phenomenon on such a scale. Covering the resulting explosion of public enthusiasm, the contemporary media initially struggled to find ways to describe the picture itself. “A cowboy movie set in space, that’s Star Wars,” pronounces the announcer in a TV news clip included in the new Nerdwriter video above. “It’s old-fashioned escapist entertainment, pure and simple.” That may have been all the Italian film industry needed to hear. The “spaghetti westerns” of the previous dozen years had proven that it could profitably master an American genre; surely it could do the same with a similar one.

Among the results, alas, one looks in vain for A Fistful of Dollars, or even a Navajo Joe. Nerdwriter creator Evan Puschak goes over various instances of shameless imitation that characterize the Italian Star Wars clones, but you don’t have to take his word for it; you can, in fact, find some of these movies on YouTube.

title: Google says Russian speakers pulled off first-ever fully automated AI cyberattack
content:
Russian-speaking hackers built an AI agent that carried out what may be the first-ever fully-automated cyberattack, Google reported Monday.

The tech giant’s cyber threat intelligence division said it had spotted hackers using artificial intelligence to “fully automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation without a human in the loop for the first time.”

The development could mark an inflection point in the use of AI for cyberattacks, which has dominated headlines and worried policymakers since AI firm Anthropic released its specialized model Mythos in April. 

Hackers, who used Russian in technical documentation identified by Google, set up a series of AI agents to “continuously compare pre- and post-patch code, identify vulnerabilities, and automatically develop exploits without human intervention,” Google said.

That means the agents independently found software flaws and ways to use them. The attackers targeted French websites in the media, entertainment and education sectors, Google said.

title: Measuring the value of public investment in open source for the European tech industry
content:
Open source powers Europe’s digital economy. A new report by the Sovereign Tech Agency and iconomy quantifies how public investment into open source strengthens European SMEs, the innovation economy and investors around them.

Europe’s digital economy runs on open source. Openly licensed software components and libraries are embedded throughout the products and services European companies rely on every day. Of the commercial codebases audited in 2026, 98% contained open source code. It is critical to the resilience, security, and competitiveness of the digital economy, but the work it takes to keep it running safely is often invisible, even to the businesses depending on it.

title: Tutkimus: Robotin välttelevä katse voi aiheuttaa ulkopuolisuuden tunnetta
content:
Johanna Kohvakka

Ihmiset suhtautuvat humanoidirobotteihin usein kuin tietoisiin toimijoihin ja tulkitsevat niiden eleitä sosiaalisina viesteinä. Katsekontaktia välttelevä robotti herätti voimakkaampia kielteisiä tunnereaktioita tutkimuksessa, joka tehtiin Tampereen yliopiston Human Information Processing -laboratoriossa.

"Ihmiset tapaavat suhtautua humanoidirobottien katse-eleisiin sosiaalisina viesteinä. Halusimme selvittää, mitä seuraa, kun robotti osoittaa välinpitämättömyyttä välttämällä katsekontaktia", tutkijatohtori Samuli Linnunsalo kertoo Tampereen yliopiston tiedotteessa.

Tutkimukseen osallistuneet olivat lyhyessä vuorovaikutustilanteessa humanoidirobotti NAOn kanssa. Robotti joko katsoi osallistujaa kohti tai vältti katsekontaktia. Tämän jälkeen osallistujat arvioivat kyselyissä ulkopuolisuuden tunnettaan, mielialaansa sekä neljän perustarpeen täyttymistä. Näitä olivat yhteenkuuluvuus, itsetunto, vuorovaikutustilanteen hallinta ja oman olemassaolon merkityksellisyys.

title: Switzerland is Prosecuting the First Journalist Under its Banking Secrecy Law. The EU Has No Comment.
content:
The unprecedented criminal prosecution of a journalist under Switzerland's stringent banking secrecy law is raising alarms among press freedom advocates across Europe. But the European Union has nothing to say about it.

Lukas Hässig, founder of the financial news website Inside Paradeplatz, was charged in October over articles published a decade ago. The articles cited leaked information, and focused on financial dealings involving former Raiffeisen Switzerland chief executive Pierin Vincenz, and his business partner Beat Stocker.

The revelations helped trigger investigations that eventually led to criminal proceedings. In April 2022, Vincenz and Stocker were convicted of fraud and other offenses. Vincenz was sentenced to three years and nine months in prison, while Stocker received a four-year term. Both have appealed, with a ruling expected in January 2027.

Separately, Stocker filed a criminal complaint asking prosecutors to pursue charges against Hässig.

"There is a public interest in the facts. An unsubstantiated, flawed narrative is another matter," Stocker told OCCRP, arguing that there was “no legal basis under Swiss criminal law” for his own conviction.

title: The antidote to TikTok tourism? A free paper map
content: Planning a city trip in Europe? Chances are you’ll scroll TikTok for ideas or ask ChatGPT to build an itinerary. But have you considered using a paper map instead? Sound old-school? It might be what you actually need. Meet USE-IT Europe, a network of free city maps made by young locals who want to share with visitors where they actually spend their time. The maps cover the usual ground – where to eat, drink, shop, relax – but each one also comes with a five-minute history of the city and an “Act like a local” section full of dos and don’ts. In Prague for example, don’t order the chimney cake. It’s “not Czech, not traditional, and not so good.” Depending on the city, you might also find Spotify playlists, useful local phrases, and suggestions on what to order at a bar or bring to a picnic in the park. The maps are full of practical tips too, from free concerts to places where you can get free tap water. “Honest tourist information from locals for young travellers. And nobody can pay to be on the map. title: Chicago Is $55 Billion in Debt, With No End in Sight. It’s a Threat to City Services.
content:
When the city of Chicago eventually finishes its spending plan for 2027, $3.9 billion will come right off the top. 

Taxpayers will have nothing to show for it. Not a single cent of that money will be used to fill a pothole, pick up a can of garbage, pay a firefighter to respond to an emergency or address lead poisoning in children. 

Strapped into a straitjacket made up of the city’s debt, there is nothing Chicago’s mayor or City Council can do about it, forced to spend billions every year simply to stay current on the $55 billion it owes to banks and its pension funds. 

No other big city will pay more toward its debt this year or next, according to an analysis by WTTW News and ProPublica. This year, $3.6 billion out of a $16.6 billion budget was consumed by debt.

New York City, with a population three times the size of Chicago’s and a budget more than seven times as big, has $47 billion in debt backed by tax revenues. Los Angeles, which has approximately 1 million more residents than Chicago but a smaller budget, has $1 billion in debt set to be paid back with taxes, records show.

title: Making injustice legal: How Israeli law legitimizes apartheid, genocide and impunity
content:
Israel’s laws are built to entrench ethnic domination, and international courts are under attack for noticing

Originally published on Global Voices

Roadblocks at the entrance to Shuhada Street in Hebron, Palestine. Photo by Travel 2 Palestine on Flickr (CC BY 2.0).

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank are subject to Israeli civil law. Palestinians who suffer their violence and occupation are subject to Israeli military law. The two face two different legal systems. 

Palestinian, Israeli and international rights groups, and UN findings, have long argued this is not a malfunction of Israeli justice but its design, and that the international system meant to check, and failed to do so, is being taken apart.

For years, Israeli military data has shown conviction rates for Palestinians in Israeli military courts to be anything between 99.74 and 96 percent.

  • Ethiopian National Defence Forces’ (ENDF) troops are now present in Gemhalo, located between Sheraro and Badme, while the Eritrean Defence Forces are reportedly stationed near Badme. 
  • Badme itself remains outside the control of any military force. Eritrean intelligence personnel have been seen in the town. 
  • Families have been displaced amid ongoing clashes in Badme, with residents stating that shops and markets have been closed.

title: Wealthy countries aren’t protected from climate extremes – Europe must adapt quickly too
content:
Extreme heatwaves across Europe led to significant annual deaths this summer. In Spain, floods in Valencia during 2024 killed 200 people and paralysed infrastructure. Germany’s 2021 floods highlighted severe weaknesses in early-warning communication, while wildfires in France led to large-scale evacuations and reduced air quality.

It’s easy to assume that strong institutions and technological capacity protect wealthy countries from the consequences of climate change. But evidence suggests otherwise. Well-resourced cities remain vulnerable to rapid-onset extremes. Our research across high-income countries identifies a fundamental challenge here: adaptation responsibility is frequently fragmented across governance levels.

The knock-on effects of climate-induced extremes also expose longstanding inequalities between people of different ages, genders and race, for example. Migrant, elderly and low-income communities are disproportionately affected by climate consequences. This is not simply because these communities are more exposed to the effects of extreme weather. Their vulnerabilities are also shaped by housing quality, income, health and lower political influence.

title: Senegalin ulkoministeri Cheikh Niang vierailee Suomessa
content:
Senegalin ulkoministeri Cheikh Niang, joka vastaa myös Afrikan integraatiosta ja ulkomailla asuvien senegalilaisten asioista, vierailee Helsingissä 18. marraskuuta ja tapaa ulkoministeri Elina Valtosen.

Ulkoministeri Valtonen ja Senegalin ulkoministeri Cheikh Niang keskustelevat maiden kahdenvälisistä suhteista, Euroopan ja Afrikan turvallisuudesta, yhteistyöstä monenvälisissä kysymyksissä sekä kaupallistaloudellisista suhteista. title: Global Warming Approaches 1.5 Degrees in "Calamity for the World's Ecosystems"
content:
As delegates, industry lobbyists and civil society activists attend this year’s United Nations climate summit, known as COP31, we speak with international environmental lawyer Farhana Yamin about the state of global climate efforts. Yamin helped write the landmark 2015 Paris Agreement and has attended 28 of the last 31 U.N. climate summits. The Paris Agreement aimed to keep global temperatures below 1.5 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels, a threshold that climate scientists say the world will now overshoot.

“It’s a moment of great sadness, actually, for the world community that we weren’t able to start the phaseout, start the acceleration of the transition away from fossil fuels 10 years earlier,” says Yamin. “So, we’re about 10 years behind, but I hope that over time that we can accelerate.”

title: Kutsu: Julkistustilaisuus Tampereella 4.12.2026 kello 10 – Erkki Karvosen kirjoittama Viestinnän perusteet ilmestyy

Emeritusprofessori Erkki Karvosen uusi tietokirja Viestinnän perusteet — Johdatus viestintätieteisiin on yleistajuinen esitys viestinnästä, sen historiasta ja teorioista. Kirja tarjoaa kattavasti lähestymistapoja viestinnän ilmiöihin ja viestinnän tutkimusaloihin, joihin kuuluvat muun muassa journalistiikka, mediatutkimus, puheviestintä, organisaatioviestintä, informaatiotutkimus, pelitutkimus, mediakulttuuri, elokuvantutkimus ja mediakasvatus.

Tervetuloa Viestinnän perusteet -kirjan julkistustilaisuuteen perjantaina 4.12.2026 kello 10 Tampereen yliopiston Café & Aula Toivoon. Tila sijaitsee Tampereen yliopiston Päätalossa, Kalevantie 4, 2. kerros. Tilaisuutta juontaa ja puheenjohtajana toimii Marko Ala-Fossi, yliopistonlehtori ja viestintätieteiden yksikönjohtaja.

title: Sähkön hinta voi moninkertaistua hetkessä – maksuton Virtanen-palvelu kertoo, mihin sähkö todella kuluu
content:
Talvi lähestyy, ja sähkön hinnan voimakas vaihtelu tekee kulutuksen ajoittamisesta taas ajankohtaista. Vuonna 2026 pörssisähkön kuukausikeskihinta on vaihdellut rajusti: heinäkuun 1,93 sentistä helmikuun 17,22 senttiin kilowattitunnilta. Vuorokauden sisäinen vaihtelu on vielä suurempaa. Marraskuun 2026 alussa päivän halvimman ja kalleimman vartin hinnan ero oli melkein satakertainen.

Nitorin data-analyytikkojen kehittämä kaikille avoin, maksuton Virtanen.ai-työkalu auttaa kotitalouksia ymmärtämään, mihin sähköä todella kuluu. Uutuutena palvelussa voi nyt verrata pörssisähkön ja kiinteähintaisen sopimuksen eroja. Virtasella voi myös selvittää, onko noin vuosi sitten käyttöön otettu varttihinnoittelu tullut omassa taloudessa halvemmaksi vai kalliimmaksi.

”Sähkön hinta saattaa moninkertaistua hetkessä. Virtasen avulla voi laskea helposti, minkälainen sähkösopimus olisi tällä hetkellä oman kulutuksen kohdalla kaikkein järkevin”, palvelun kehittämisestä vastannut Nitorin data-asiantuntija Esa Puttonen kertoo.

title: Liberia Lifts a Major Barrier to Education
content:
“Our children are able to go to school again.” That's how one Liberian parent described the impact of a new government policy banning school registration fees for kindergarten through sixth grade. The policy is already helping families who struggled to pay the fees, removing a longstanding barrier to their children's education.

Since the policy took effect in September, Liberian child advocates have interviewed parents in four counties to assess whether schools were complying with the ban. The findings offered encouraging early indications: nearly all 20 parents interviewed knew about the policy and had enrolled their children without paying registration fees.

Parents described the difference the policy was making. “The decision by the ministry is so good,” said a parent in Bong County. “It enables our children to go to school free without worry.” Another parent whose children had previously been out of school said, “For some of us that don’t have money, it helps us a lot.”

title: How Leo Tolstoy Became a Vegetarian and Jumpstarted the Vegetarian & Humanitarian Movements in the 19th Century
content:
Leo Tolstoy is remembered as both a towering pinnacle of Russian literature and a fascinating example of Christian anarchism, a mystical version of which the aristocratic author pioneered in the last quarter century of his life. After a dramatic conversion, Tolstoy rejected his social position, the favored vices of his youth, and the dietary habits of his culture, becoming a vocal proponent of vegetarianism in his ascetic quest for the good life. Thousands of his contemporaries found Tolstoy’s example deeply compelling, and several communes formed around his principles, to his dismay. “To speak of ‘Tolstoyism,’” he wrote, “to seek guidance, to inquire about my solution of questions, is a great and gross error.”

“Still,” writes Kelsey Osgood at The New Yorker, “people insisted on seeking guidance from him,” including a young Mahatma Gandhi, who struck up a lively correspondence with the writer and in 1910 founded a community called “Tolstoy Farm” near Johannesburg.

title: EU sanctions Russian trolls, hackers
content:
European Union member countries on Monday issued sanctions against a Russian company running disinformation campaigns and one of Russia’s most well-known hacking groups.

The Council of the EU said it had sanctioned the Social Design Agency, a Moscow-based firm that carries out “large scale information manipulation and interference projects,” as well as 24 of its staff members.

The Social Design Agency is “funded, directed and supervised” by the Russian government and has organized disinformation campaigns targeting EU countries, EU institutions and European support for Ukraine, Council said.

The group has been connected in the past to a vast online disinformation network known as Doppelganger. It targeted the 2024 European elections and carried out “dedicated operations against EU member states such as Germany and France,” countries said.

EU capitals also agreed to levy sanctions against notorious Russian hacking group NoName057(16), which has targeted government bodies and critical infrastructure as well as private firms in the EU, Ukraine and the United States.

title: Kenen ehdoilla Suomea rakennetaan?
content:
Tekoäly muuttaa maailmaa nopeammin kuin ehdimme sitä ymmärtää. Puhutaan murroksesta, jota verrataan teolliseen vallankumoukseen. Se vaikuttaa siihen, millaista työtä teemme, miten turvallisuudestamme huolehditaan ja kenellä on valtaa. Tämä murros ei tapahdu vain jossain pilvessä. Sen fyysinen muoto on datakeskus: valtava halli, joka tarvitsee maata, sähköä, kriittisiä raaka-aineita ja usein vettä.

Juuri nyt maailmalla on käynnissä datakeskusbuumi, ja Suomi kiinnostaa. Meillä on vakaa yhteiskunta, toimiva sähköverkko, viileä ilmasto ja puhdasta, edullista energiaa. Siksi kansainväliset jättiyhtiöt katsovat tänne.

Se ei ole ongelma sinänsä, mutta ongelma on siinä, kenen ehdoilla jättiyhtiöiden datakeskuksia nousee Suomeen – kenen ehdoilla Suomea rakennetaan. Datakeskukset voivat tuoda Suomeen työtä, osaamista ja verotuloja, mutta jos annamme niiden tulla millä ehdoilla tahansa, havahdumme liian myöhään seurauksiin. Silloin metsät, vedet ja yhteinen sähkömme muuttuvat raaka-aineeksi, josta hyöty valuu muualle ja haitat jäävät tänne. Siksi meillä vihreillä on selkeä kanta: Suomi ei voi olla datakeskusten villi länsi.

title: KI & Wahlen
content:
Die meisten Menschen finden Informationen im Internet über die Online-Suche. Dort treten zunehmend generative Antworten an die Stelle einer Liste von Links, während Originalquellen in den Hintergrund geraten. Zusätzlich steigt die Zahl der Menschen, die sich direkt bei Chatbots informieren. Wie eine Antwort zustande kommt, welche Quellen sie stützen und wie verlässlich sie ist, bleibt bei diesen KI-Systemen oft unklar.

Diese Entwicklung ist aus mehreren Gründen problematisch. Sie schwächt die eigenständige Meinungsbildung, denn Nutzer*innen lesen eine vermeintlich vermeintlich umfassende generierte Antwort, statt selbst auf Originalquellen zu klicken. Zugleich gefährdet sie das Informationsökosystem: Wenn Nutzer*innen seltener Medienseiten besuchen, gerät deren Refinanzierung unter Druck. KI-Systeme sind jedoch darauf angewiesen, dass Medien und andere Quellen verlässliche Informationen veröffentlichen, damit sie selbst hochwertige Antworten liefern können. Auf lange Sicht kann das den Informationszugang der Menschen gefährden – eine wichtige Vorbedingung für eine funktionierende Demokratie.

title: Cycling Connects: Bringing Tourism and Transport Together for a More Connected Baltic Sea Region
content:
Almost 80 participants joined the “Cycling Connects” webinar on 26 October 2026, marking the first jointly organised thematic event by the EU Strategy for the Baltic Sea Region (EUSBSR) Policy Areas Tourism and Transport. The strong interest and lively exchange confirmed that cycling tourism is much more than a tourism product – it is an important link between sustainable mobility, regional development and cross-border cooperation.

The webinar brought together representatives of the European Commission, European cycling organisations, regional authorities, tourism stakeholders and EU-funded projects to exchange perspectives, showcase practical initiatives and explore how closer cooperation between tourism and transport can support a more sustainable and accessible Baltic Sea Region.

Cycling tourism is growing in importance across Europe, offering opportunities to encourage low-carbon travel, connect urban and rural destinations, support local businesses and develop attractive cross-border tourism experiences. Yet unlocking its full potential requires cooperation across sectors, administrative borders and policy areas.

title: Three of the Financial Sins That Left Chicago $55 Billion in Debt — and Counting
content:
Chicago’s finances have long been strained by soaring pension expenses, spiraling personnel costs and a massive amount of debt. Budget deficits and financial crises now arrive with regularity, as city leaders face crucial decisions on how to dig out of this financial mess. 

The track record of decision-making within City Hall suggests that avoiding hard choices for expediency leads to trouble. 

The city must spend billions every year from its main account — known as its corporate fund — to keep current on the $55 billion it owes to banks and its pension funds. The debt consists of $19 billion in loan payments that must be repaid by revenue from property and sales taxes as well as $36 billion to ensure former employees get retirement benefits. The city also borrows money to make improvements to its water and sewer systems and to fund operations at its airports, but that debt is repaid with fees, not money from the corporate fund. 

Here are three of the big decisions Chicago officials have made over the years that dug the city into such a massive financial hole.

title: People's Climate March: Thousands Demonstrate in Turkey as Country Hosts COP31 U.N. Summit
content:
Democracy Now! is in Antalya, Turkey, where this year’s United Nations climate summit, COP31, is being held. For the second year in a row, the United States has not sent an official delegation to the international talks, in keeping with the Trump administration’s longstanding hostility to such efforts to address the climate crisis.

There are nearly 100,000 participants here at this year’s climate summit, including many civil society activists from Turkey and around the globe. Over the weekend, Democracy Now! was in the streets of Antalya to speak with some of the thousands of protesters who marched to demand urgent climate action, including many labor leaders.

“Trade unions care about a lot more than just protecting jobs. We have systemic demands,” said Lala Peñaranda, the Latin America coordinator for Trade Unions for Energy Democracy.
